title: Designing for the Working Mind
author: Chris Jones
summary: Jones applies Cognitive Load Theory to school curriculum design, arguing that the aim is not to make learning easier but to direct pupils' limited working memory toward meaningful thinking. He summarises intrinsic, extraneous and germane load with the goals of managing, minimising and maximising each. He argues that curriculum coherence, uncluttered materials and good sequencing reduce avoidable cognitive burden. He also connects overload to disengagement and to equity, since disadvantaged pupils are hit hardest by fragmented design. The move is to treat teachers as cognitive designers and to recast coherence as an ethical issue.
points: Working memory is finite, so schools that overload pupils with disconnected demands undermine learning regardless of motivation.
The three load types have distinct goals: manage intrinsic load, minimise extraneous load and maximise germane load.
Curriculum coherence and sequencing reduce cognitive friction, and progression should be judged by cognitive readiness rather than coverage.
Cluttered slides and over-supporting can increase cognitive burden, and cognitive exhaustion is often misread as unwillingness.
Disadvantaged pupils are disproportionately affected by fragmented design, making coherent curriculum an ethical matter.
quotes: Working memory is finite, fragile, and easily overwhelmed. Yet schools often design learning experiences as though attention, processing capacity, and retention are unlimited.
Over the years, I have worked with many schools where pupils were not struggling because they lacked ability, but because the cognitive demands placed upon them had become fragmented and excessive.

Extraneous load, however, is different. This is the cognitive burden created by poor design: confusing instructions, fragmented resources, inconsistent layouts, unnecessary distractions, or poorly sequenced explanations.
The schools that manage this well tend to think carefully about progression. Not simply coverage, but cognitive readiness.
Good design is rarely about adding more. It is usually about removing what is unnecessary.
I have worked with schools where pupils appeared reluctant learners, only for it to become clear that the issue was not unwillingness, but cognitive exhaustion.

Pupils from disadvantaged backgrounds are often disproportionately affected by fragmented curriculum design and excessive extraneous load because they may have fewer opportunities to compensate outside school.
The goal is not to make learning easier. It is to make thinking possible.
